parole.significato: A Dutch and German measure of liquids, used in England for Rhine wine, varying in different cities, being in Amsterdam…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch aam, from Latin ama, a variant of hama, from Ancient Greek ἄμη (ámē, “bucket”).

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Geranium found throughout the temperate zone.
parole.testo: First attested in the 1500s. Calque of Dutch craenhals; cognate with German Kranichhals and Middle Low German kraneshals, all likely derived from Latin geranium, from Ancient Greek γέρᾰνος (gérănos, “crane”). parole.significato: A sea or lake voyage, especially one taken for pleasure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch kruisen (“cross, sail around”), from kruis (“cross”), from Middle Dutch cruce, from Latin crux.

parole.significato: A gadget, device, or object whose name is either unknown, forgotten, or omitted for the purpose of humor.
parole.testo: Probably of multiple origins. Partially a borrowing from Dutch dinges (“thingamajig, thingy; whatshisname, whatshername”), ding (“thing”). parole.significato: A kind of coarse woolen cloth, having a thick nap or frieze.
parole.testo: From Dutch duffel, named after Duffel, a town in Belgium, itself ultimately from Latin Dubrolocus, the first particle from Gaulish dubrum.

parole.significato: A former Dutch unit of distance, usually equivalent to about 3 miles or 5–6 km.
parole.testo: From Dutch mijl, cognate with English mile and similarly derived from Latin milia (“Roman mile, 1000 Roman paces”) but used instead for the much longer league of about an hour's walk.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch patroon (“patron saint; boss”), from Middle Dutch patroon, from Latin patrōnus (“protector; patron”). Doublet of padrone, patron, Patronus, and pattern.

parole.significato: A net or dragnet used for trawling.
parole.testo: 16th century, borrowed from Dutch tragelen (“to pull with a towline, trawl”), from Middle Dutch traghelen, from traghel (“dragnet”) (presumably from Latin tragula (“dragnet”)), and as such root-cognate with English drag and dray.
